title: Visual Perception & Displays I

sentences.text: Hello and welcome to the NPTEL MOOC's course on Foundations for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems.
Today we are going to start a new lecture on visual perception and displays.
Before we start, as is the practice we are following, let us quickly recap what we have learned in the previous few lectures.
So, we talked about the human factors.
How they are relevant and why they are relevant?
Because we are dealing with interactive systems.
XR systems are essentially interactive systems and human factors play an important role in their design.
We have also seen how human physiology dictates how AR/VR systems should be designed, and how they are related.
But that discussion was at a very broad level.
Now, we are going into a little more detail with respect to each of our senses and how those are useful for the design and implementation of extended reality systems.
So, in this lecture, what we are going to learn about is how our visual senses work and how they determine how to design the visual experience while dealing with extended reality systems.

So, essentially we are going to cover the basics of light, lenses and our eyes, and also how these concepts are going to help understand the working of head-mounted displays and other displays that are relevant for immersive experiences.
Now, let us quickly have another look at why we should know all these things.
This knowledge is crucial to understand how VR headsets work.
Now, of course, it may come to your mind why we are emphasizing VR headsets only when we are dealing with a vast subject covering all extended reality systems and all types of displays.
The reason is simple: when we talk of visual displays, visual senses, and we talk of immersive experiences, then the thing that comes to our mind immediately is the headsets, VR headsets.
So, essentially, we will be trying to understand in a little more detail how these headsets work.
Earlier, we talked about the hardware, the sensors, and other things.
Now, we will try to understand the headsets from the point of view of how they work and why they work.
What in our, physiology as well as our behavior makes it work.

And we need to know this because we know that light is emitted from the displays and arrives on our retinas, which is part of our eye, and in VR headsets, a system of both engineered and natural lenses guides the light and eventually that leads to visual perception.
Now, when I say both engineered and natural, so two types of lenses I mentioned here, engineered lenses and natural lenses.
Now, engineered, of course, we understand is the part of the headset; natural means parts of the eyes.
So, our eyes also contain lenses, as we all know.
When we combine these two lenses, these two types of lenses, the combined system essentially helps us perceive the immersive visual content.
So it is important to know how the light propagates through this combination of lenses and eventually leads us to perceive the scene.
There are other reasons also, apart from how perception works.
Another reason can be understanding the construction of virtual worlds.
So how is that so?
With this knowledge, we can understand the physics of light propagation and accordingly we can model that physics in the virtual worlds that we are using, we are experiencing.
Also, we can determine what should be rendered on the visual display depending on this knowledge.
Such knowledge is also helpful to understand camera working, how the camera works.

Once we know how the light propagates, how our lenses work, then we will also be able to understand how the camera setup works and accordingly in a virtual world we can decide the camera position for the best experience.

So, it provides this knowledge, provides another way to present a virtual world through panoramic videos based on our idea of how camera works, how our eyes work and accordingly how we will be able to receive the videos.
Cameras are also important for tracking.

So, once we know the working of a camera, it will help us build tracking hardware and software in a better way rather than trying to build it without knowing anything about the vision, about the working of our visual sense.

So those are the reasons, multiple reasons for acquiring the knowledge of how our visual system, visual sense works, how the light propagates, how it propagates through the lenses, through our eyes, how it gets interpreted to let us perceive the scene and so on.
That is the knowledge we are looking forward to.
Now let us start our discussion on on basic light behavior.

moving through space at high speeds.

The retina is composed of optic nerve fibers and photoreceptors.
So, if you recall our earlier discussion, we said that visual perception requires the bodily sensors that are called photoreceptors.
So, those photoreceptors are part of the retina, which is on the back side of the eye.
And the retina also contains optic nerve fibers, that is the neurons that take it to the brain, take the signal to the brain.
Now, there are two types of photoreceptors: rods and cones.
So, the human eye contains two types of photoreceptors: rods and cones.
Rods are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina, and cones are mainly in a small central region of the retina, which is called the fovea.
So, we have optic nerves shown here, which take the signal to the brain.

can share an optic nerve which aids in sensitivity to lower levels of light.

So, when we perceive something only with cones, vision accomplished only with cones, that is photopic vision.
And when we perceive something with rods only, that is scotopic.
So, scotopic is more related to the peripheral vision, photopic is more related to the direct vision or central vision.
We perceive colors only in the photopic vision.
So, when we say that we are perceiving color, we have to keep in mind that that is due to the photopic vision accomplished with cones.
In scotopic vision, weak lights are visible as a series of grays.
So, color perception is not that good.
So, photopic vision gives us a sense of color.
So, how is color perception related to the light which we have discussed so far?

with a frequency of 4.3 into 10 to the power 14 hertz and wavelength 700 nanometer.

between red and violet, that is called visible light and we are able to perceive visible light using our photopic vision.

Central and peripheral, these two types of vision are supported by human eyes.

Now, this region where photoreceptor density is less, with a mix of rods and an even lesser amount of cones, is the peripheral region of our eyes, and that leads to peripheral vision.
Now, we are much better at detecting movement in our periphery but cannot distinguish colors effectively.
So, that is a very interesting thing.
When we try to detect movement, the peripheral region, or peripheral vision, is better than central vision.

roadmap.lecture_goal: understand the fundamental principles of light propagation and the physiological processes that enable visual perception.

objectives.text: You'll be able to justify the study of visual perception and light propagation, and compare the various physical descriptions of light and how it interacts with surfaces.
You'll be able to trace the path of light through the eye, explain the mechanisms of color perception, and compare the functions of different visual components and types of vision.

segments.subgoal: Justify the study of visual perception and light propagation in XR systems

key_points.text: The lecture will cover how our visual senses function and how this knowledge informs the design of visual experiences in extended reality systems.
Visual perception in VR headsets is achieved through the combined action of engineered lenses (in the headset) and natural lenses (in the eyes).
Understanding light propagation allows developers to model physics accurately within virtual worlds and determine what should be rendered.
Knowledge of camera and visual sense working is crucial for building effective tracking hardware and software.

key_terms.definition: Visual perception is the process where light arrives on the retina, which is part of the eye, leading to the perception of the scene. This process is guided by both engineered and natural lenses.
Natural lens is the part of the eyes that is used in the combined lens system. Our eyes naturally contain lenses that contribute to visual perception.
Light propagation is the movement of light through the combination of lenses. This process eventually leads to the perception of the scene.
Combined system is the combination of engineered and natural lenses. This dual system essentially helps the user perceive the immersive visual content.

segments.subgoal: Compare the particle, wave, and ray descriptions of light and their applications

key_points.text: Light can be described as photons, tiny particles of energy, which is helpful for understanding light received by a sensor or receptor.
Light can be described as waves, which are ripples through space, and this description is helpful in understanding the spectrum of color.
Light can be described as rays, which are trajectories assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon, and this view helps explain how lenses work.

key_terms.definition: Photons are tiny particles of energy that move through space at high speeds. This particle view of light is helpful when calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.
A wave is a ripple that travels through space. This description of light as a wave is helpful for understanding the spectrum of color.
A ray is a trajectory or path assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon. This concept of light as a ray is helpful in explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

segments.subgoal: Describe the three ways light interacts with material surfaces

key_points.text: Transmission occurs when light passes through the material and exits the surface.,,
Absorption occurs when light rays terminate within the material, meaning there is no further propagation outside the object.,,
Reflection happens when a ray falls on the surface and bounces off without penetrating the object.
Light rays can be reflected, absorbed, or transmitted, and all three processes can happen simultaneously.,,

key_terms.definition: Transmission is the phenomenon where a part of the light ray passes through the material surface and exits the object. This process differs from absorption, where the light rays terminate within the material.
Absorption occurs when a portion of a light ray is absorbed within the material, causing the ray to terminate inside the object. There is no further propagation of the ray outside the material.

Reflection is the phenomenon where a light ray strikes a surface and bounces away without penetrating or entering the object. This process distinguishes it from transmission, where the light passes through the material.

segments.subgoal: Explain the mechanism of color perception using direct and ambient light sources

key_points.text: Color perception occurs when light reflects from a surface point and reaches the viewer's eye.
The perceived color is determined by the intensity of the light that reaches the viewer's eye.
Ambient light is light reflected from surrounding objects in the environment, mixing with direct light.
The final color is determined by the intensity of the combined light from both the direct source and the ambient light.

key_terms.definition: Color perception is the process where a viewer perceives a color based on the intensity of light that reaches their eye. This light is determined by how light rays interact with the surface of an object.
Ambient light is the light present in the environment that reaches the eye. This light is reflected from the object surface and combines with light coming from a direct source.

segments.subgoal: Trace the path of light and explain how the eye focuses images onto the retina

key_points.text: Light rays reach the eye after getting reflected from surfaces.
Light passes through the cornea, pupil, lens, and finally the retina.
The cornea and lens refract light to focus images onto the retina.
Light propagation through the eye can be understood in terms of light as ray and transmission of light rays.

key_terms.definition: Cornea is an outer surface component of the eye that refracts light rays as they pass through it.
Lens is a component of the eye that refracts light rays, working in sequence with the cornea to focus images.
Retina is a component located at the back side of the eye where the light rays are focused to form images.
Transmission is the process where light falls onto a surface, passes through the medium, and subsequently emerges from that surface.

segments.subgoal: Describe the structure and function of the eye's visual components

key_points.text: The iris controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.
Light travels through the cornea and lens before reaching the retina.
The retina contains photoreceptors and optic nerve fibers that transmit visual signals to the brain.
The retina contains two types of photoreceptors, rods and cones, which are distributed differently (rods in periphery, cones in fovea).

key_terms.definition: Retina is the part of the eye located on the back side, which is composed of optic nerve fibers and photoreceptors.
Photoreceptor is a bodily sensor required for visual perception.
Iris is the structure that controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.
Rods are a type of photoreceptor that are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina.
Cones are a type of photoreceptor that are mainly located in a small central region of the retina, which is called the fovea.

segments.subgoal: Compare how rods and cones contribute to different types of vision

key_points.text: Light passes through several semi-liquid materials, such as aqueous and vitreous humor, when propagating through the eye.
Rods can share an optic nerve to aid sensitivity in low light, whereas cones generally have one optic nerve fiber each to aid image resolution.
Photopic vision, accomplished with cones, allows for color perception and is related to central vision.
Scotopic vision, accomplished with rods, is related to peripheral vision and results in weak lights being visible as grays.

key_terms.definition: Photopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with cones, which allows for the perception of colors and is associated with central vision.
Scotopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with rods, which is related to peripheral vision and allows weak lights to be visible as a series of grays.
Image acuity is the ability to perceive fine detail, which is aided by having one optic nerve fiber for each cone.

segments.subgoal: Explain how the range of visible light frequencies leads to color perception

key_points.text: Visible light is defined as a spectrum of electromagnetic light waves within a specific frequency range.
The visible spectrum ranges from red light (4.3 x 10^14 Hz, 700 nm) to violet light (7.5 x 10^14 Hz, 400 nm).
Color perception, known as photopic vision, occurs when light waves within the visible range excite the cones in the eye.
Light outside the visible range cannot excite the photoreceptors (cones), meaning no color perception occurs.

key_terms.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves. This range encompasses the light waves that fall between the red and violet ends of the spectrum.

Photopic vision is the perception of color that occurs when light waves within the visible range excite the cones in the eye. This process is dependent on the light falling within the red-to-violet spectrum, as light outside this range cannot activate the photoreceptors.
Cones are photoreceptors in the eye that are excited by light waves within the visible range. Excitation of these cones is what gives us the perception of color.

segments.subgoal: Compare and contrast central and peripheral vision based on photoreceptor density

key_points.text: The two types of vision (central and peripheral) are determined by the density of photoreceptors across the retina.
Central vision is supported by the fovea, a central retinal region with the greatest concentration of cones.
To perceive a sharp color image, the eyes must be focused and pointed straight at the target due to the nature of central vision.
Peripheral vision occurs in regions of the retina with low rod and cone density, making it better for detecting movement but poor for color perception.

key_terms.definition: Fovea is the central region of the retina that possesses the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, specifically cones. This region is responsible for contributing to the perception of central vision.

Central vision is one of the two types of vision supported by human eyes, which is enabled by the high concentration of cones found in the fovea. This type of vision allows the perception of a sharp color image when the eyes are pointed straight at a target.

Peripheral vision is the other type of vision supported by human eyes, which relies on the peripheral region of the retina. This region has a lower density of photoreceptors and is better at detecting movement than central vision.
Cones are photoreceptors that are highly concentrated in the innermost part of the fovea. These cones are responsible for contributing to the idea of central vision and perceiving sharp color images.

segments.subgoal: Explain the physiological cause and function of the blind spot

key_points.text: The blind spot is a region of the retina that lacks photoreceptors, meaning light falling there does not lead to perception.
The blind spot exists because the density of the optic nerve prevents photoreceptors from being placed in that specific region of the retina.
The previous discussion covered the nature of light, how it propagates, and how the eye processes light.
The next part of the lecture will apply this knowledge to understanding the working of immersive headsets and displays.

key_terms.definition: Blind spot is a region in the eye where the individual cannot perceive light or visual stimuli. This area is blind because it lacks photoreceptors.

Photoreceptor is a component of the retina that is necessary for visual perception. Photoreceptors are involved in receiving light, and their absence in certain regions prevents the perception of visual stimuli.
